profiled_workloads.selection_reason: Lowest-speedup timing workload (0.230) and the smallest slab (2048 fp16 elements, 8KB moved): boundary of the tiny-copy regime.
Second-lowest-speedup timing workload (0.452) at 32768 elements; same tiny regime with 16x the data, used to test size-independence.
Best-speedup control workload (1.688) in the mid regime (524288 elements, 2MB moved) to establish where the candidate already beats the reference.
Near-parity boundary workload (1.043) where the round-1-to-2 gain stalled; probes whether the large-slab ceiling is memory or scheduling.
Highest-latency float16 workload (0.0776 ms, 134MB moved); extreme of the large regime.
Highest-latency workload overall (0.2169 ms) and below-parity (0.996); doubling of bytes per element at the largest slab tests bandwidth scaling.
Tiny-slab control in a second dtype (0.536) to check that the tiny-regime signature is dtype-independent.
Tiny-slab control in a third dtype (0.465) to confirm the sub-1us vector work / scalar-dominated signature.

findings.label: Mid and large slabs run at the memory-system rate that the reference also reaches; the remaining ceiling is memory, not index arithmetic
findings.backend_detail: Ascend msprof op_summary: aiv_mte2_ratio / aiv_mte3_ratio are the AIV load/store pipeline busy fractions; Task Duration is per-launch device duration.

evidence.metric: aiv_mte2_ratio (load pipeline busy fraction) for float16::3
aiv_mte3_ratio (store pipeline busy fraction) for float16::3

findings.inference: Using bytes moved = 2 x (out-slab bytes) and the mean kernel durations, the candidate device rates are float16::2 0.80 TB/s, float16::3 3.19 TB/s, float16::4 1.71 TB/s, float32::4 1.23 TB/s. Applying the identical byte model to the eval reference latencies in the round-2 context (4.373 / 10.983 / 90.486 / 216.100 us) gives reference rates of 0.48 / 3.05 / 1.48 / 1.24 TB/s. The candidate/reference rate ratios 1.67 / 1.05 / 1.16 / 0.99 reproduce the measured eval speedups 1.688 / 1.043 / 1.167 / 0.996, so these four workloads are limited by the same memory path in both implementations and their speedups are capped by the memory system rather than by the kernel's index arithmetic. The high MTE2/MTE3 occupancy (0.86/0.73 and 0.93/0.60) confirms the load/store pipelines are the busiest units. The 3.19 TB/s in float16::3, well above a plausible HBM rate for this part, suggests its 33.6MB working set is largely L2-served (device reports 176MB L2), whereas float32::4 moves 268MB and is DRAM-bound at 1.23 TB/s.

findings.label: Tiny slabs are fixed-cost bound: kernel duration is independent of a 16x data difference and is dominated by non-vector overhead
findings.backend_detail: Ascend msprof: aiv_vec_time/aiv_scalar_time are per-launch AIV pipeline busy times; vec_ratio 1% with scalar_ratio 40-51% indicates an issue-bound, not datapath-bound, kernel.

evidence.metric: Task Duration(us) mean/min/max, Block Num for float16::0
Task Duration(us) mean/min/max, Block Num for float16::1
aiv_time(us) vs Task Duration(us) for float16::0
Task Duration(us) mean/min/max, Block Num for float32::0
Task Duration(us) mean/min/max, Block Num for bfloat16::0

findings.inference: float16::1 moves 16x the bytes of float16::0 (128KB vs 8KB) yet its mean device duration is only 4% higher (1.476 vs 1.416 us), and the same ~1.4-1.5 us duration appears at grid=1 in three different dtypes (1.416 fp16, 1.517 fp32, 1.415 bf16). The vector pipeline is busy for only 8 ns of that window (aiv_vec_time 0.008 us, ratio ~0.012) while scalar issue occupies 40-51% of the reported AIV window; at 8KB per direction in 1.416 us the effective rate is ~0.006 TB/s, about 500x below the mid-slab rates, so no part of this time is data-dependent. Between 0.53 and 0.63 us of each launch lies outside the AIV busy window (Task Duration 1.416 vs aiv_time 0.883), so per-launch dispatch plus a fixed per-program prologue dominate, and with grid=1-8 the small path leaves most of the 20 reported AI cores idle. The round-2 eval latency at float16::0 (2.437 us) is even larger than the profiled mean (1.416 us), which places the whole deficit against the 0.559 us reference in per-call fixed cost rather than in copy work.

findings.label: Exposed instruction-fetch/issue latency in the tiny kernels (icache misses and a 3.7x per-launch spread)
findings.backend_detail: Ascend msprof aiv_icache_miss_rate per invocation; tiny kernels show non-zero miss rates where all mid/large kernels show 0.0.

evidence.metric: per-invocation aiv_icache_miss_rate values within the float16::0 profile
evidence.value: 0.185 on the majority of the slower invocations, 0.0 on the fastest ones

evidence.metric: Task Duration(us) min vs max for float16::0

findings.inference: A ~5.5% instruction-cache miss rate appears only in the tiny one-program launches and is exactly 0.0 for every slab of 524288 elements or more; within the float16::0 profile the slower invocations carry a 0.185 miss rate and the fastest ones 0.0, and the same launches vary 3.7x in duration (1.04-3.84 us). This is consistent with the remaining cost being instruction fetch/issue latency of the kernel prologue and loop machinery being exposed when there is no data-level work to hide it, rather than with any data movement cost. Confidence is medium because msprof does not attribute the missing 0.53 us between Task Duration and aiv_time to a specific pipeline.

performance_interpretation: Round 2 (geo_mean 0.0103 -> 0.8126) confirms the first half of the frozen hypothesis: the per-element runtime division and the 8192-program splitting loop are gone, mid/large slabs are now truly bandwidth-bound, and their speedups (1.51-1.69 on 2MB slabs, 1.04-1.08 on 33.6MB, 1.00-1.17 on 134-268MB) are quantitatively explained by candidate/reference device rates that agree within 0-17%. The hypothesis is falsified for the six smallest timing workloads, which are not bandwidth-bound at all: they move 8-128KB in 1.42-1.48 us regardless of size (16x data costs +4% time), spend only 8 ns in the vector pipeline, 40-51% of their AIV window in scalar issue, and 0.5-0.6 us of each launch outside the AIV window. Their eval latencies (1.2-2.4 us against a 0.56-0.9 us reference) are therefore pure per-call/per-program fixed cost. Because the geo_mean is bounded by those six workloads (geometric mean of the six tiny speedups is 0.435 while the other nine average 1.233), the experimental budget should now go to the fixed cost of the small-size path, not to further work on the slabs that already sit on the memory roofline. The profiler also shows that simply adding programs does not help the tiny path (grid=8 at float16::1 is no faster than grid=1 at float16::0), so the target of the next experiment is the per-program prologue/loop machinery and the per-call launch cost, not the grid geometry.

next_experiment.action_description: Make the small-size path (n <= 65536 elements) a straight-line, loop-free copy: one fixed small BLOCK (e.g. 512 elements, chosen so BLOCK divides the common run lengths) with grid = ceil(n/BLOCK) bounded by the vector-core count, no tl.range grid-stride loop, no masks on divisible sizes, single launch per call. Keep the existing float16::2/::3/::4 and float32::4 path (n > 65536) unchanged so the memory-roofline workloads are untouched. The decisive probe is float16::0 and float32::0: the existing kernel needs 1.42-1.52 us for 8KB with grid=1, so if a loop-free single-program straight-line copy at BLOCK=2048 lands well under that (toward 1.0 us or below) the cost is this kernel's prologue and the change should be applied to all n <= 65536; if the minimal kernel still measures ~1.4 us, the limit is per-call dispatch outside the kernel and the current solution should be kept as final rather than micro-optimized further.
next_experiment.expected_impact: Profile-derived: the 0.53-0.63 us between Task Duration and AIV busy time plus the 0.33-0.36 us scalar prologue are the target; if the prologue is the cause, tiny-slab device time drops from 1.42-1.52 us toward ~0.9-1.1 us, lifting the six tiny workloads from an average speedup of 0.435 to roughly 0.6-0.75 and the headline geo_mean from 0.813 to about 0.90-1.00 (to reach geo_mean 1.0 the tiny six must average 0.73). The mid/large workloads are memory-roofline limited and are expected to stay at 1.04-1.69.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: Risk: a separate small-size branch can accidentally capture the 524288-element workload (currently the best win, 1.688) or slow it through extra host-side branching, and the loop-free kernel can lose contiguous-coalesced behaviour if the fixed BLOCK does not divide the run length (masks reappear). Mitigation: keep the n > 65536 path byte-identical and verify float16::2/::3/::4 with msprof Task Duration before accepting. Rollback: restore the round-2 candidate (solution sha256 13ae374623323582649495f6d5771a7ef55de882a7f21fe50751119e01343969); the change is local to the small-size branch. If the minimal straight-line kernel does not move the ~1.4 us floor, abandon this direction (do not sweep BLOCK/grid sizes) and freeze the current solution.
success_criteria: Full evaluation reports PASSED for all 33 workloads (18 correctness + 15 timing) with the frozen fingerprint re-verified.
Headline geo_mean > 0.82 (no regression against round 2's 0.8126) and the primary target geo_mean >= 0.90.
The six tiny timing workloads (float16/float32/bfloat16 ::0 and ::1) average speedup >= 0.60, up from 0.435, with each individually above its round-2 value.
No timing workload regresses by more than 2% versus round 2, in particular float16::2 (1.688), float16::4 (1.167) and bfloat16::4 (1.131).
msprof verification on float16::0 shows the mean narrow_copy Task Duration falling below 1.20 us (from 1.416 us); if it does not move, record the negative result and freeze the current solution.

warnings: msprof timing is diagnostic and does not replace eval latency; all speedup, latency and reference numbers come from get_profile_context round 2.

Tiny-slab measurements (1.02-1.5 us) are near the msprof and benchmark timing resolution; the size-independence conclusion rests on consistent means across three dtypes rather than on any single number.

Effective-bandwidth figures use a transferred-byte model (out-slab read + write) rather than a measured DRAM/L2 counter, and the L2-residency explanation for the 3.19 TB/s float16::3 rate is an inference, not a measured counter.
open_questions: The msprof mean at float16::0 (1.416 us) is below the eval latency reported for the same workload (2.437 us) while for float16::1-::4 and float32::4 the two agree within 2%; the source of this gap at the smallest shape is unresolved, so tiny-shape conclusions are qualitative rather than quantitative.

Whether the ~1.0-1.4 us floor at n <= 4096 is a device launch floor or this kernel's prologue cannot be separated without a minimal-kernel variant; every observed launch of the tiny kernels bottoms out at 1.02-1.04 us across three dtypes.

The profiler exposes only grid sizes (1/8/32/42/170), not the runtime-queried vector-core count; grids 42 and 170 are not multiples of the reported 20 AI cores, but the measured 3.19 TB/s on float16::3 (grid 42) shows wave quantization does not dominate there, and no per-wave per-block timing was extracted from the execution trace to confirm a tail effect.

msprof records ~126-200 us between successive launches of the profiled loop while eval latency is 1.2-2.4 us, so the profiled run cannot characterize the host-side per-call cost; whether the reference's 0.559 us latency at float16::0 is device-only or reflects a cheaper call path is unknown.
